name: Software Design and Engineering
description: An integrated study curriculum across the supplied software engineering and testing archive: requirements, modeling, architecture, design, teamwork and evolution, systematic testing, delivery, and responsible evaluation of development tools. Original cases connect design decisions with observable quality.
limitations: CSE13B is a merged course. This curriculum covers the supplied CSE2115 SEM and CSE1110 SQT predecessor material; it does not claim a verified final CSE13B syllabus or examination specification.

The supplied README explicitly leaves merged-course assessment, oral-presentation requirements and depth of inherited advanced topics unconfirmed. Communication practice is included as a useful inherited skill, not a mandatory CSE13B assessment.

Past SEM exams span older formats and are used for topic/problem-style evidence only. SQT exams and exercises are supplied mainly as Markdown WebLab exports; their copied solutions are not treated as authoritative new marking schemes.

All problems and lesson prose are newly authored. Open design, diagrams, proofs and test/code-writing responses are ungraded and require rubric-based self or instructor review; no code or arbitrary user input is executed.
PDF locators use one-based physical pages. Text extraction, content sampling and selected visual checks were used; not every source page was visually reviewed.

Historical tool names, organizational examples and AI claims in source slides are context, not verified current recommendations. The material teaches durable reasoning rather than current product capabilities.

topics.name: Requirements and stakeholder discovery
topics.description: Turn stakeholder needs into verifiable requirements, priorities and acceptance scenarios.

skills.name: Elicitation
skills.description: Select techniques and include overlooked stakeholders.

skills.name: Verifiable requirements
skills.description: Separate services from quality constraints and remove ambiguity.

skills.name: Prioritization
skills.description: Use priorities with context, evidence and traceability.

lesson.title: Discover the problem before the feature
paragraphs: A stakeholder can influence requirements, be affected by the system, or have responsibility for operating it. Interview end users, support staff, administrators and people with accessibility needs; a purchaser's perspective is not the whole workflow. Contextual inquiry combines observation with questions about why the current work is done that way.

Interviews reveal detail, surveys reach broader groups, prototypes make assumptions tangible, and scenarios expose exceptions. Ask for a recent concrete case, including its initial state, actions, failure paths and desired outcome. Record unresolved disagreements instead of silently choosing a requirement on behalf of all parties.

lesson.title: Make success observable
paragraphs: A functional requirement describes a service or response, such as canceling an eligible reservation. A quality requirement constrains operation, such as response time under a specified load. User requirements communicate goals; system requirements add enough precision to support design and verification. A quality label alone does not make a requirement measurable.

Worked rewrite: 'Search should be fast' becomes 'For the agreed 50,000-record dataset and 100 concurrent users, at least 95% of title searches shall return results within 500 ms during a ten-minute test.' The threshold is an example to negotiate, not an established course or product requirement. Specify empty queries, unauthorized access and failures separately.

lesson.title: Priorities and traceability
paragraphs: MoSCoW ranks needs relative to a delivery timebox: Must, Should, Could and Won't this time. Calling every item Must removes the method's value. Kano analyzes how the presence and absence of a feature affects satisfaction; a basic expectation may not delight users but still be essential.

Trace a stakeholder need to a requirement, implementation issue and acceptance test. For a booking system, 'avoid double booking' may lead to a concurrency rule, transactional design and a test where two clients compete for the last slot. Breaking work into tickets should preserve this connection to the intended outcome.

exercises.title: Find missing stakeholders
exercises.prompt: A university room-booking team interviews only lecturers. Name four other stakeholder groups, explain a distinct concern for each, and choose one elicitation technique for an overlooked workflow.
exercises.explanation: Different groups encounter conflicts, maintenance outages, support failures and access barriers that a lecturer-only interview may omit.
rubric: Identify groups such as students, facilities staff, support and users with accessibility needs.
Connect each group to a specific need or constraint.
Choose a technique with a reason, such as observing room changeovers.

exercises.title: Repair an ambiguous requirement
exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'the application must be reliable and quick' into two independently verifiable requirements. State measurement conditions and identify assumptions requiring stakeholder agreement.
exercises.explanation: A latency percentile under load and a recovery or availability target can be tested separately; vague adjectives cannot.
rubric: Separate performance from reliability/availability.
Specify measurable targets, workload/window and failure definition.
Label chosen numbers as proposed assumptions rather than discovered facts.

exercises.title: Requirement classification
exercises.prompt: Which statement most directly specifies a functional service?
exercises.explanation: Exporting a user's booking list is observable system functionality.

options.text: 95% of searches finish within 500 ms under a stated load.
The monthly service availability target is 99.5%.
An authenticated user can export their own bookings as CSV.
The deployment must fit in 2 GB of memory.

exercises.title: Resolve priority inflation
exercises.prompt: All 30 backlog items are marked Must for a two-week release. Describe a prioritization workshop that produces a defensible release scope without silently dropping an accessibility requirement.
exercises.explanation: Must is a release constraint, not a synonym for desirable. Ethical and user needs require evidence-based discussion, not automatic demotion.
rubric: Agree on release goals, capacity and consequences of omission.
Challenge Must labels through concrete scenarios and dependencies.
Discuss accessibility with affected stakeholders and record explicit decisions and deferred scope.

exercises.title: Trace a concurrency requirement
exercises.prompt: An initially available room slot receives two valid simultaneous reservation requests during healthy operation. The system must make successful progress while ensuring at most one confirmed reservation per room and time interval. Propose an acceptance scenario and name the observable outcomes.
exercises.explanation: A test that submits requests one after another misses the concurrency risk that motivates the requirement.
rubric: Create competing requests for the same slot.
Require exactly one confirmation and a clear rejection/conflict outcome for the other.
Check persistent state, not just two success/failure messages.

skills.name: Model semantics
skills.description: Distinguish multiplicity, ownership, include and extend.

skills.name: Audience and abstraction

lesson.title: Model only what answers the question
paragraphs: Use-case diagrams show actors and system goals, not internal method-call order. An include relationship represents required reused behavior; extend adds conditional behavior at an extension point in a base use case that is meaningful on its own. Actor roles need not correspond one-to-one with named people.

Class diagrams describe types, associations and multiplicities. In an association Customer 1 to Order 0..*, each Order has one Customer while a Customer may have many Orders. Composition means strong whole-part ownership and lifecycle dependence; use an ordinary association when the part exists independently or is shared.

lesson.title: Worked interaction model
paragraphs: For a checkout sequence, draw Customer, Checkout, Inventory and Payment lifelines. Checkout first reserves stock, then requests payment, then confirms the order. Use alternatives for unavailable stock and declined payment. The declined branch must release the reservation; a diagram containing only the happy path hides that obligation.

Sequence diagrams emphasize messages among participants over time. Activity diagrams emphasize control flow, decisions, forks and joins. A decision selects one path using guards; a fork starts concurrent paths and a join synchronizes them. Joining alternative paths as though both must occur can model an impossible wait.

lesson.title: Zoom and communicate
paragraphs: C4 moves from system context to containers, components and code. A C4 container is an application or data store, not necessarily a Docker container. A context diagram for a booking system can show students and an external identity provider without exposing implementation classes.

For a nontechnical stakeholder, begin with their concern, show only relevant system boundaries and explain labels. For a developer, include contracts, multiplicities and failure behavior. A useful presentation links each design choice to evidence and a tradeoff, cites sources, and makes questions and uncertainty visible; it does not prove its quality by diagram density.

exercises.title: Read multiplicity
exercises.prompt: An association places '1' at the Customer end and '0..*' at the Order end. What does it mean?
exercises.explanation: Multiplicity at an end counts possible instances at that end for one instance at the opposite end.

options.text: Each Order has one Customer; each Customer may have zero or more Orders.
Each Customer has exactly one Order.
An Order may have any number of Customers.
Customers and Orders have identical lifecycles.

exercises.title: Include or extend?
exercises.prompt: A base 'View article' use case works without translation. A user can optionally request translation while viewing. Explain an appropriate extend relationship and contrast it with required authentication in a protected checkout.
exercises.explanation: The relationship describes required versus conditional use-case behavior; it is not selected merely because one action happens later.
rubric: Model optional translation as extending View article under a condition.
Explain that protected checkout can include required authentication behavior under the specified scenario.
Distinguish optional extension from an implementation call graph.

exercises.title: Draw a failure-aware sequence
exercises.prompt: Describe or write text UML for stock reservation followed by payment. Include the payment-declined branch and the externally visible final state.
exercises.explanation: A successful reservation is not a completed checkout. The failure branch must undo or expire the reserved resource.
rubric: Provide participant lifelines and ordered reserve/pay/confirm messages.
On decline release stock and report failure without a confirmed order.
Name return values/guards sufficiently to distinguish branches.

exercises.title: Choose the right view
exercises.prompt: A university administrator wants to know which external systems receive booking data. Which view is the best starting point?
exercises.explanation: A context view explains system boundaries and external relationships at a suitable level.

options.text: A full class diagram with private fields.
A system context diagram with labeled data relationships.
A CPU instruction trace.
A diagram of every unit test.

exercises.title: Explain a design decision
exercises.prompt: Prepare a short spoken outline proposing a queue for slow report generation to nontechnical course staff. Include user benefit, one tradeoff, a visual idea and a question you would invite.
exercises.explanation: Audience adaptation and evidence matter more than architectural vocabulary. This is inherited communication practice, not a confirmed CSE13B presentation requirement.
rubric: Lead with staff/user needs and explain asynchronous completion plainly.
State a real cost such as delay, status tracking or retry handling.
Use a simple request-to-report visual, support claims and invite a relevant question.

topics.name: Architecture and quality tradeoffs
topics.description: Choose system boundaries and communication styles from quality requirements, including distributed failure behavior.

skills.description: Match layers, MVC, pipelines and events to responsibilities.

skills.name: Architecture decisions
skills.description: Document a scenario, alternatives and consequences.

lesson.title: Architecture captures costly decisions
paragraphs: Architecture describes important components, responsibilities and relationships. A layered design separates presentation, application/domain behavior and infrastructure; MVC separates model, view and controller concerns. These divisions can support independent reasoning, but a layer that merely forwards every call may add ceremony without useful responsibility.

A pipe-and-filter architecture fits a stream transformed through stages with clear input/output contracts. Publish-subscribe decouples producers from consumers through event channels, but introduces questions about delivery, ordering, duplicate processing and failures. Patterns describe tradeoffs in context, not universal upgrades.

lesson.title: Worked choice: a student booking service
paragraphs: A small team with shared release cadence can start with a modular monolith: bookings, identity adapters and notifications have explicit internal interfaces while deployment stays simple. Split services when independent ownership, scaling or failure isolation provides a concrete benefit that outweighs network and operational complexity.

Suppose sending email is slow and should not block confirmation. Publish a BookingConfirmed event after reliable persistence and let a notification consumer process it. Retrying an event may deliver it twice, so the consumer needs an idempotency rule. A queue moves failure handling; it does not make failure disappear.

lesson.title: Distributed tradeoffs and evidence
paragraphs: During a network partition, a distributed service cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and successful responses to every request. This is the useful scope of the CAP tradeoff, not an unrestricted 'choose any two at all times' slogan. Some domains can tolerate temporarily stale displays; others must reject uncertain updates.

Write an architectural decision record with context, constraints, alternatives, decision and consequences. Use quality scenarios: a stimulus under stated conditions produces a response measured by a target. For example, a worker outage should delay emails without losing confirmed bookings. Validate with a fault experiment or test rather than treating a diagram as evidence.

exercises.title: Choose a pipeline
exercises.prompt: A tool reads sensor records, validates them, converts units and aggregates hourly values. Which style most directly supports reusable sequential transformation stages?
exercises.explanation: Each stage transforms a well-defined stream for the next stage.

options.text: A single global mutable singleton.
An inheritance tree for every file.
Pipe-and-filter.
An unstructured set of cross-calling components.

exercises.title: Justify a deployment boundary
exercises.prompt: A three-person team proposes 12 microservices for an early booking product. Evaluate this choice using two possible benefits, three concrete costs and evidence that could justify starting with a modular monolith.
exercises.explanation: Service count is not a quality metric. Independent deployment is valuable only when its benefits exceed coordination and operational costs.
rubric: Mention independent scale/ownership or isolation as conditional benefits.
Discuss network failure, deployment/observability, contract/data consistency costs.
Tie the choice to actual team size, workload and change/release needs.

exercises.title: Duplicate event handling
exercises.prompt: A notification consumer receives the same BookingConfirmed event twice after a retry. Propose an idempotency strategy and explain what must be persisted.
exercises.explanation: Deduplication must survive restarts. External side effects require an explicit retry/idempotency design.
rubric: Use a stable event or business-operation identifier.
Persist processed/sent state with an appropriate atomicity policy.
Discuss the send-and-record failure window rather than assuming an in-memory set is enough.

exercises.title: CAP in context
exercises.prompt: Two replicas are partitioned. A booking service must prevent conflicting confirmations for the last seat. Explain a possible availability tradeoff and why 'choose two' is an incomplete explanation.
exercises.explanation: Continuing to accept conflicting writes on both sides sacrifices the chosen consistency guarantee.
rubric: Restrict or reject writes where authoritative agreement is unavailable.
Explain the partition-specific conflict between consistency and availability.
Separate this from normal-operation latency and other quality attributes.

exercises.title: Write a bounded decision
exercises.prompt: Write a concise decision record for keeping report generation in a background worker. Include context, an alternative, two consequences and one measurable validation scenario.
exercises.explanation: A reviewable decision names both the benefit and what the team must now operate and test.
rubric: State the slow-report/user-response problem and why a worker fits.
Compare synchronous generation or another plausible alternative.
Include status/retry complexity and a concrete response or recovery experiment.

topics.name: SOLID, contracts and substitutability
topics.description: Use responsibility boundaries and behavioral promises to make designs extensible and testable.

skills.name: Design principles
skills.description: Apply cohesion, interface segregation and dependency inversion.

skills.name: Behavioral contracts
skills.description: Specify preconditions, postconditions and invariants.

skills.name: Substitutability
skills.description: Check inherited promises without strengthening caller obligations.

lesson.title: Principles guide change boundaries
paragraphs: Single responsibility means a coherent reason to change, not one method per class. Open/closed design isolates a likely variation behind an interface so a new implementation does not require editing all clients. Interface segregation keeps clients dependent on the operations they actually need.

Dependency inversion makes high-level policy depend on abstractions instead of concrete infrastructure. Dependency injection supplies those collaborators from outside; it is a construction technique, not the same concept. A booking rule can depend on a ReservationStore interface, implemented by a database adapter and a test fake.

lesson.title: Worked account contract
paragraphs: For withdraw(amount), a possible precondition is 0<amount<=balance, a postcondition is balance'=old(balance)-amount, and an invariant is balance>=0 at public method boundaries. If the public API instead promises an exception for invalid amounts, that error behavior belongs in the specification and should be tested.

Invariants can be temporarily false inside a carefully controlled operation but must hold when the object is observable through its public boundary. Java assertions may be disabled, so do not rely on them for always-required input validation. Exceptions and explicit checks can enforce public error behavior; contracts still describe what those checks mean.

lesson.title: Subclasses must keep promises
paragraphs: A subtype cannot demand more than the base method's precondition from existing callers. It may accept more inputs, and it must provide at least the promised postcondition. Preserving a method signature is insufficient if behavior changes incompatibly.

Example: a base withdraw accepts any positive amount up to balance. A subtype that rejects all amounts below 10 strengthens the precondition and breaks a client that legally withdraws 5. A subtype that additionally logs successful withdrawals can strengthen behavior without invalidating that client's expectations, provided the original success and failure semantics remain.

exercises.title: Separate reasons to change
exercises.prompt: A Report class calculates totals, renders HTML and sends SMTP messages. Propose a responsibility split and explain which dependency direction keeps calculation independent of email infrastructure.
exercises.explanation: Tax or aggregation changes should not require changing SMTP setup; delivery details should not dictate the total-calculation contract.
rubric: Separate calculation, formatting and delivery concerns.
Keep domain policy independent of SMTP-specific classes.
Explain benefits through independent change/test scenarios rather than number of classes.

exercises.title: Write a postcondition
exercises.prompt: For a nonnegative account balance and valid withdraw(amount), state precondition, postcondition using old balance, and class invariant. Specify one boundary test.
exercises.explanation: A relational postcondition checks the transition, not just that the resulting balance is nonnegative.
rubric: Require amount>0 and amount<=old balance under the cooperative contract.
Require new balance=old balance-amount and nonnegative invariant.
Start with a positive balance, withdraw exactly that balance, and check that the result is zero.

exercises.title: Subtype restriction
exercises.prompt: A base method accepts all nonempty strings. A subtype accepts only strings of length at least 8. Which principle is violated for callers using the base contract?
exercises.explanation: The subtype rejects inputs that were legal under the base promise.

Liskov substitutability through a stronger precondition.
Stable sorting.
Dependency injection necessarily.

exercises.title: Always-on validation
exercises.prompt: A public method must reject invalid booking dates in every deployment. Why is a Java assert statement alone insufficient, and what should the API specify instead?
exercises.explanation: A required production check must not depend on the assertion-enabled runtime flag.
rubric: Assertions can be disabled.
Use explicit validation with documented exception/error behavior.
Test invalid dates and ensure no partial booking state survives rejection.

exercises.title: Segregate an interface
exercises.prompt: A ReadOnlyArchive implementation must implement delete() only to throw UnsupportedOperationException because clients share a giant Archive interface. Propose smaller interfaces and explain how this improves substitutability.
exercises.explanation: A capability-specific interface avoids promising a deletion operation the object cannot support.
rubric: Separate read operations from mutation capabilities.
Type read-only clients against the read interface and mutating clients against the write-capable interface.
Explain that advertised operations should have satisfiable contracts.

topics.name: Behavioral design patterns
topics.description: Separate interchangeable algorithms, notification and traversal responsibilities without hiding control flow.

skills.name: Pattern selection
skills.description: Distinguish Strategy, Observer, Iterator and Chain of Responsibility.

skills.name: Collaborations
skills.description: Describe roles, call flow and lifetime hazards.

lesson.title: Strategy isolates a changing algorithm
paragraphs: A Strategy interface represents one interchangeable behavior. A route planner delegates computeRoute to a walking or driving strategy while retaining stable orchestration. This can remove a growing conditional, but only helps when variation is real; tiny fixed cases do not automatically need a class hierarchy.

An Iterator exposes traversal without exposing representation. Different iterators can traverse the same tree in depth-first or breadth-first order. Each iterator needs its own cursor and a defined policy for collection mutation. The collection should not store one shared traversal cursor used by all clients.

lesson.title: Observer communicates a change
paragraphs: A subject keeps observers that wish to receive change notifications. A score model can notify a table view and chart without knowing their display details. The observer interface decouples notification from the reaction; subscription and unsubscription still require lifecycle management.

Worked scenario: a view subscribes when opened, updates on score changes, then unsubscribes when closed. If it remains registered, it may receive stale updates or be retained in memory. Notification order, reentrant changes and exceptions in one observer need explicit policies. Observer within one process is not automatically a reliable distributed message broker.

lesson.title: Chain of Responsibility makes ordered handling explicit
paragraphs: A chain passes a request through handlers. One variant stops at the first handler that handles it; another performs a sequence of validations and stops on failure. State which semantics apply. An authorization-then-format-validation pipeline differs from a fallback chain of support desks.

A useful pattern explanation names the client, interface, concrete collaborators and message sequence. For a validation chain, each validator returns a result or forwards to next; the terminal case must accept or reject explicitly. Changing handler order can change behavior, so treat ordering as part of the contract and test it.

exercises.title: Select an algorithm at runtime
exercises.prompt: A delivery planner must switch between walking and cycling routing rules without changing request validation. Which pattern best isolates the route calculation?
exercises.explanation: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a shared operation.

exercises.prompt: A dashboard opens and closes repeatedly but keeps receiving duplicate notifications. Explain a likely Observer lifecycle bug and propose both a repair and a regression test.
exercises.explanation: Decoupled notification does not remove lifecycle obligations; retained subscriptions can duplicate effects and retain obsolete views.
rubric: Identify repeated registration or missing unsubscription.
Return/dispose a subscription or make registration policy explicit.
Open/close/reopen and verify only current observers receive one notification.

exercises.title: Independent iteration

exercises.explanation: A shared cursor makes one client's next call skip data for the other.
rubric: Each client needs independent progress.
Collection creates separate iterator objects holding their own cursor.
Define end-of-iteration and mutation behavior.

exercises.title: State chain semantics
exercises.prompt: Design a booking-validation chain for authorization, valid dates and capacity. Specify stopping behavior and a test proving unauthorized requests do not query capacity.
exercises.explanation: Order can encode meaningful cost and access constraints; the chain must have observable failure semantics.
rubric: Name handlers and order.
Stop immediately with an explicit failure on authorization rejection.
Verify the capacity collaborator is not called for unauthorized input while a valid request reaches it.

exercises.title: Strategy or Observer?
exercises.prompt: A teammate proposes Observer to choose one compression algorithm for each export. Explain the mismatch and a better pattern, including the caller-to-collaborator flow.
exercises.explanation: Selection of a behavior and notification of an event solve different coordination problems.
rubric: Choosing one calculation is Strategy, not broadcasting a change.
Exporter delegates compress(data) to the chosen strategy.
